articles.title: Satellite images verify new strikes on two Russian airbases
articles.body:
- Satellite images confirmed Ukrainian FP-1 drones destroyed an ammunition depot and maintenance facility and damaged two radars at Russia's Millerovo airbase on August 30.
- Separate imagery from a September 4 strike showed a destroyed Ka-52 and Mi-28 helicopter and a damaged Mi-8 at Sochi's airport.
Satellite imagery has confirmed damage to two radar systems, a maintenance facility and an ammunition depot at Russia’s Millerovo airbase in Rostov Oblast, following a Ukrainian drone strike on the night of August 30, according to images published by the Dnipro OSINT.
Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi reported that Ukraine’s 1st Separate Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces carried out the attack using FP-1 long-range strike drones, also striking Yeysk airbase the same night. At Millerovo, the satellite images show the ammunition depot and the base’s technical and maintenance facility, known by its Ukrainian abbreviation TECh, were completely destroyed, while an RSP-27 precision approach radar and a Nebo-SV early warning radar were both damaged.
Millerovo has been struck repeatedly since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. The base sits about four kilometers northwest of Millerovo city and has hosted Russia’s 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment, which flies Su-30SM fighters, along with earlier deployments of Su-25 attack aircraft. Ukrainian officials have described the base as a key staging point for Russian frontline aviation supporting operations in eastern and southern Ukraine, and it was previously hit in drone attacks in December 2023 and July 2025.
The FP-1 is built by the Ukrainian company Fire Point and has become one of Ukraine’s primary tools for long-range strikes inside Russia. The drone carries a warhead of 60 to 120 kilograms depending on configuration, with a documented range of 1,600 kilometers, and Fire Point has said an upgraded model unveiled this year can reach as far as 2,700 kilometers. Ukraine’s military has credited FP-1 strikes with more than half of its long-range drone missions against Russian targets, including ammunition depots, oil refineries, radar stations and air defense systems.
Separately, satellite and visual evidence reviewed following a strike on September 4 identified damage to Russian military aircraft parked at Sochi’s airport in Krasnodar Krai, according to the same reporting.
A Ka-52 attack helicopter and a Mi-28 attack helicopter were destroyed, and a Mi-8 transport helicopter was damaged, at the facility’s military helicopter parking area. Sochi’s airport has been targeted in prior Ukrainian strikes, including an October 2023 attack that Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence directorate said hit a parking area for Russian helicopters in the airport’s Adler district, and an August 2025 strike that set fire to a nearby oil depot.
Russian authorities have not issued a public statement on either the Millerovo or Sochi strikes described in this report.

articles.title: US withdrawal from Iraq will be watched closely by Iran-backed militias, Kurds - analysis
articles.body:
The US is to meet a September 30 deadline for withdrawing from Iraq, Kurdish media outlet Rudaw reported on Sunday.
It was one of several reports that indicate the US is committed to taking away air defense systems from the Kurdistan Region. The full details of this are unclear and hard to confirm. What matters is not necessarily if it is accurate, but that people will think it is happening.
Rudaw wrote, “The United States will withdraw its defense systems from the Kurdistan Region along with its remaining troops by the end of September under an agreement with the Iraqi government, a senior Iraqi security official said on Sunday.”
The report noted that “Qasim al-Araji, security advisor to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, told Rudaw that the withdrawal includes all defense systems, including remaining ones in Erbil, adding that the phased removal of troops and military equipment has already begun.”
Araji said, “On September 30, coalition forces will completely withdraw from Iraq, and this is the implementation of the agreement made between the previous government and the global coalition…The American side has expressed its full readiness to implement the agreement and withdraw by the specified deadline.”
US pressuring Iraq to control militias
This comes as the US is also pressuring Iraq to rein in Iranian-backed militias and disarm them. So far, none of the militias have disarmed. It doesn’t seem possible that any weapons will be collected in September. If no militias were disarmed in the last months, why would they hand over their guns now?
Instead, what they will do is put more conditions on disarmament. Some may also claim they already put their guns under “state control.” Most of the militias are part of the Baghdad-backed Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF). As such, they will claim the PMF controls their weapons already. This is a kind of bait and switch.
Rudaw said there is progress with the militias. “Araji said discussions with the armed groups were moving in a positive direction.”
Araji said, “After the withdrawal of the coalition, an agreement will be reached on a comprehensive mechanism to place all weapons under the control of the state and the commander-in-chief of the armed forces.” He added that “discussions are proceeding very well and there is positive understanding.”
It’s worth noting that the militias were supposed to hand over their weapons by September 30. Now the handover is overdue. This is how the can gets kicked down the road.
For the Kurdistan Region, this is a problem because the militias and Iran have already targeted the region with more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks since February 2026.
Iran has even targeted the offices of the Kurdish Regional Government’s prime minister and president. Iran is indicating that it wants to strike at dissident groups in the Kurdistan Region and also that it can do as it wants.
Not clear if air defenses will remain
In the past, reports said that US and coalition air defenses had downed some of the drone attacks. It is not clear if some of the defenses will actually remain. The US has a large consulate in Erbil. It is logical that the US will want to defend it. The consulate, as well as a UAE consulate, has been targeted in the past.
Yet, Rudaw said, “the US has already relocated eight Patriot surface-to-air missile batteries to Jordan, while Britain has transferred its Rapid Sentry system to Cyprus.”
The report added context, noting the “US and British forces have defended Erbil airport and surrounding areas using anti-missile and counter-drone systems stationed at the base. Despite those defenses, at least five American soldiers and contractors have been killed in attacks in recent months, Rudaw understands.”
The report also names five Iranian-backed militias as refusing to disarm. These include Kataib Hezbollah, Sayyid al-Shuhada and Harakat al-Nujaba. Kataib Hezbollah is believed to be the most dangerous in terms of its threat and close ties to the IRGC.
In 2020, when the US killed IRGC Quds Force head Qasem Soleimani, he was riding with Kataib Hezbollah leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis. Muhandis was also killed.
Kataib Hezbollah killed three Americans in Jordan in a drone attack in 2024. It has also attacked Saudi Arabia. The militias, such as the three mentioned above, often play a role in the “Islamic Resistance” in Iraq, which has carried out attacks on Israel, the US, and others in recent years.

articles.title: View from Russia: Experts on why Kushner and Witkoff came to Moscow
articles.body:
View from Russia: Experts on why Kushner and Witkoff came to Moscow
The latest visit to Moscow by Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff has triggered a fresh wave of speculation in Russia about what Washington is really trying to achieve.
With US President Donald Trump under pressure at home and much of his administration’s foreign-policy bandwidth consumed by Iran, the trip has been interpreted less as a breakthrough mission than as a signal – one that may be aimed as much at domestic American politics and alliance management as at Russia itself.
Russian analysts see the visit in different ways. Some believe the Americans are simply sounding out Moscow before returning to Kiev, trying to gauge whether any space remains for movement on Ukraine. Others argue the mission is part of a broader performance of diplomatic activity by the Trump White House, intended to project momentum where little real progress is possible. Still others view it as an exercise in ‘shuttle diplomacy’, useful mainly for information-gathering and atmospherics rather than for producing concrete results.
Roman Romanov, American studies specialist, lecturer at the Faculty of International Relations, Political Science, and Foreign Regional Studies at RSUH
I have two explanations regarding the visit and the format of this visit. First, the American side has already shown several times that it is interested in maintaining dialogue with both Moscow and Kiev. And this visit – or rather, this tour – is aimed at “synchronizing watches.” What does that mean? The Americans are trying to understand what conditions might be acceptable to the parties for resuming an active negotiating process. In other words, what can be offered to both sides so that they are prepared to move the dialogue in the direction of progress.
The second explanation is purely domestic-political for the United States. Against the backdrop of the failure of the Iran campaign, it is necessary to demonstrate some other kind of political activity that at least theoretically resembles progress with a concrete result. Trump has done this kind of thing more than once.
Do they have any ready-made proposals? I do not think so, because, first, at the moment a significant part of US foreign-policy resources is concentrated on Iran, and second, because despite the constructive role of both Witkoff and Kushner, they still act more as envoys of the American president on a specific issue than as direct participants formulating the American president’s position on this issue.
It is difficult to explain why they first went to Moscow and then to Kiev. One can assume they first want to hear Moscow’s stance, because it is in a more advantageous position – Russia is advancing, winning on the battlefield – so the US believes it would be more expedient first to hear out Moscow’s demands and gauge how much they’ve changed since August 2025, since the meeting in Anchorage.
At the same time, although we do not observe public participation by the EU, through closed channels the European Union surely communicates its interests. Their representatives are not there, but the position the Americans are shaping includes the EU’s position as well.
Dmitry Dtobnitsky – Russian political scientist specializing in American studies, expert in US foreign and domestic policy
These negotiations will continue – that’s the only perspective they have. What are we negotiating with the US about? About how to stop the conflict in Ukraine? Let’s be serious. First, this conflict is much broader than Russia’s military operation. It is a geopolitical conflict with very high stakes, the kind that happens with Europe once every several decades or even centuries. The Cold War period with the US was still an exception in that there were at least attempts to play at détente from time to time.
The world has entered an era of major transformation. In that sense, the narrow focus is – will they reach an agreement on Ukraine? No. Every time you think about that, you have to recall how it all started, why it is like this, how wrongly the world is structured, how important it is for Russia to insist on its interests, why the European bureaucracy itself cannot accept that, because otherwise that would mean the end of both it and the political class of many countries. Why can’t this conflict stop? Because it can’t be settled. Someone has to win. Just as with the US and Iran (which, incidentally, is a much more local conflict) – it is impossible to agree, there can be no deal. There can only be some movement in which one of the sides explicitly or implicitly recognizes its defeat. It may not be total defeat, but at least at some stage one side wins and the other side does not recognize it. Such a process will last a long time, but in the end there will still be some de facto consolidation of the results of this conflict. Not a negotiated one, unfortunately, but a factual one. Diplomats may formalize such a conclusion, or they may not. Frankly, that is no longer important.
When we talk about Russia-US negotiations on Ukraine, there are two extremes, and both miss the essence. Yes, we are negotiating, and we constantly demonstrate that Russia and the US have nothing to fight over. We are ready to coexist with the US on the same globe. That is exactly why Putin says: “Of course, Kushner and Witkoff are welcome guests, come. What else should we show you from Moscow’s kitchen?” You see, the US cannot conduct negotiations on Ukraine because it cannot force either Kiev, London, or Brussels to accept Russia’s reasonable demands. And how are they going to pressure Russia? I think the Trump administration more or less understands that it is pointless. So what kind of negotiations on Ukraine can there be?
Some say [Russian Finance Minister] Siluanov and [US Treasury Secretary] Bessent will come to some understanding, and perhaps there will be incredible financial, economic, or investment cooperation between the US and Russia. I have said many times that there can be no serious cooperation between Russia and the US. There are neither material nor geopolitical grounds for it. Are we now supposed to throw away all the achievements of localizing our civilian aviation industry and start buying Boeing again? Are we going to hand over half of the most convenient Arctic territory on the planet to the US? Is that it? Or are we going to sell all Russian oil through Mr. Kushner? How do you imagine that? Some say: “Investments will come here.” But that would mean that instead of creating a sovereign financial system, we would say: “No, let’s reintegrate ourselves back into the collapsing dollar system. Let’s support it with our achievements of the past five years.” It’s obvious that there can be no real cooperation.
One can have symbolic cooperation. It is a wonderful look when two great countries can do something together. The most we will get is a hockey match and an ‘Apollo-Soyuz’. It must be understood that these are purely token steps, which only demonstrate that nothing particularly substantial can happen. It does not mean it will be forbidden. It simply will never play a substantial role. Even in 2019, before Covid and the military operation, trade turnover between Russia and the US was negligibly small. And that is understandable: it is geopolitics, geoeconomics – you cannot jump over that. And now, after so much effort has been spent to become independent and to work with Eurasia on a new basis, to say, “No, now let’s start doing something again with the Americans” is just laughable. That will not happen.
Andrey Manoylo, doctor of Political Sciences, professor at Moscow State University, head of the Department of Information and Hybrid Wars at APN Alter
Why did Kushner and Witkoff fly to Moscow for the sixth time? It’s both simple and complicated at the same time. Kirill Dmitriev, being one of the corners of the ‘Anchorage triangle’ (a configuration of three equidistant centers of power – [Foreign Minister] Sergey Lavrov, [Kremlin aide] Yury Ushakov, Dmitriev), is a red rag both for Ushakov, the “social architect” of Anchorage, and for the more skeptically minded Sergey Lavrov. Especially given his ability to remain in the media spotlight.
That is precisely why the visit of Witkoff and Kushner – direct competitors of the ‘triangle’s’ hardline diplomacy – may have been planned as a simple diversion: to annoy those with whom [CIA chief] John Ratcliffe had contacts in Moscow. To show that the ball is now in Dmitriev’s court.
In all seriousness, though, Witkoff and Kushner did not bring anything strategic to Moscow. Their direct and, most likely, only task is to gather feedback from Ratcliffe’s visit.
Dmitriev is a gifted figure, but he is not an intelligence officer with an innate poker face, nor is he a career diplomat. Dmitriev is a living person, he is talkative, and “a chatterbox is a godsend for a spy.” I am convinced these two are flying in with an intelligence questionnaire. They will extract all the information from Dmitriev – what people are talking about in the president’s circle, rumors, gossip, among which there will also be leaks of genuinely secret information.
Ratcliffe made a lot of noise. His visit is still agitating minds; some see in him almost a messenger of the Apocalypse. It is no coincidence that people immediately started talking about mobilization – which in reality is “utter nonsense” (as our president said), about some secret Security Council meetings right in the middle of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, and even about war with Norway. It is obvious that Ratcliffe stirred something up, and the American duo came to find out how ready that brew is. They have no other tasks.
And one more important point. What Witkoff and Kushner are doing now with Dmitriev is the well-known practice of ‘shuttle diplomacy’. We know it from the events preceding the collapse of the Soviet Union. The author of the term was Henry Kissinger, who once bought Mikhail Gorbachev’s trust by saying: “Gorby, while you and I are trying to break the ice of hatred, our foreign ministries with their slowness are ruining everything – they are slowing down the reset of our relations. Let’s push them aside and solve things directly. We are not stupider than our subordinates, are we?” Gorbachev happily agreed, realizing that by removing the Foreign Ministry from the talks, he was ridding himself of criticism – no one would contradict him. But practice showed that the Foreign Ministry was the very mechanism that protected against hasty decisions, even if they seemed correct and the only possible ones. Gorbachev lost, and together with him the entire Soviet Union lost.
And this is not the only case that confirms the rule: however attractive ‘shuttle diplomacy’ may look, it always leads to defeat, and defeat leads to catastrophe. Having such rich historical experience and so many examples, we still continue enthusiastically to play at ‘shuttle diplomacy’ with Kushner and Witkoff. Why? That’s a good question.
Gevorg Mirzayan, specialist in American studies
The US began sending signals about its readiness for dialogue after Russia sharply intensified its retaliatory strikes on Ukraine and put the Kiev regime before the inevitable catastrophe of the coming winter. It is possible the Americans will ask us to stop, and then Trump could show voters, before the congressional elections, a nice picture of his successful peacekeeping mission.
The meeting between Bessent and Siluanov at the G20 summit also fits into this scheme – no serious issues were raised there; the important thing was to demonstrate the positive attitude of the US administration toward bilateral interaction.
Well, we are ready for peace in Ukraine, but only on our own terms – and those terms are unchanged and well known to Washington.
Yegor Tropov, political scientist specializing in American studies
The latest visit by the American negotiating delegation is primarily a symbolic step toward restoring dialogue and laying the groundwork for the future development of relations between Russia and the United States. In the four-sided diplomatic process, it is the American side that is most interested in the quickest possible signing of a peace document – though one that is more formal and declarative than a genuine and lasting peace.
For the sake of media image and his political role as the chief mediator, Donald Trump is ready to conduct numerous negotiations that verbally move towards peace, whereas in reality what leads to peace is only the lack of political will, finances, and weapons on the part of Europe and Ukraine to continue resisting – resources they still have enough of for years to come.
At the same time, one should not underestimate the importance of symbolism in the art of diplomacy: interstate communication, the establishment and strengthening of professional and personal relationships can play a much more significant role in the future – under conditions of a full-scale warming of interstate relations and the resumption of full-fledged economic and political cooperation.

articles.title: US aircraft carriers within Iran's reach
articles.body:
Amid the intensifying military confrontation between Iran and the United States, the news of Iran firing ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer is not merely a development on the battlefield; it could be a sign of a shift in the operational environment for American forces and an increase in the cost of Washington's military presence in the region's waters.
The US Central Command (CENTCOM) has announced that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer, and that these vessels managed to survive several attacks. According to the American account, none of the US forces were harmed in these attacks.
At first glance, the most important question might be whether the missiles actually struck the American ships. But from a strategic perspective, the significance of this development goes beyond the extent of direct damage. The more important issue is the change that such attacks can create in the calculations of American commanders regarding the level of security and freedom of action of US naval vessels in the region.
An aircraft carrier is one of the most important instruments of US military power projection beyond its borders. By deploying an aircraft carrier and its accompanying strike group, Washington in effect moves a portion of its air and naval power to the closest possible point to a crisis. This presence is intended to create deterrence, strike capability, and the ability to react quickly for the United States.
But this same feature also brings a vulnerability; the closer a carrier is to a conflict zone, the more important its protection becomes, and more resources must be allocated to defend it.
A carrier strike group is not limited to the carrier itself. A collection of destroyers, air defense systems, fighter jets, early warning and reconnaissance aircraft, and other military equipment are responsible for its protection. Therefore, a missile threat against an aircraft carrier effectively means challenging a vast defensive network.
From this angle, even if the launched missiles are intercepted and no damage is inflicted on the carrier, the attack itself can have operational consequences. Because American commanders must assume that their vessels are within range and that any presence in the region faces the possibility of attack. This is what can be called the "cost of presence."
To change the other side's calculations, Iran does not necessarily need to destroy a US carrier in every attack. Increasing the cost of protecting carriers, limiting their freedom of movement, changing the operational distance, increasing the need for reconnaissance, and creating psychological pressure on forces deployed in the region can also be part of the deterrence objective.
In modern warfare, a weapon is sometimes effective when it forces the opposing side to engage a large set of resources and equipment to counter it. From this perspective, a ballistic missile is not just a tool for inflicting damage; it can also be a tool for changing the operational behavior of the opposing side.
Of course, one should not conclude from this incident that the military balance between Iran and the United States has changed. The United States still possesses significant superiority in various military, intelligence, air, and naval domains, and its aircraft carriers have multiple layers of defense. Therefore, a distinction must be made between the "ability to target" and the "ability to destroy" a military target.
What matters now is the repeatability of this threat. If American forces conclude that the presence of aircraft carriers in certain areas continually exposes them to missile attacks, they will be forced to review their deployment and operational patterns.
In such circumstances, the distance of carriers from coastal areas, their movement patterns, the level of escort, the number of protective fighter jets, and the volume of reconnaissance operations could change. Each of these changes would mean an increase in operational costs for the United States.
On the other hand, the US response is also noteworthy. Washington will attempt to show, by responding to Iranian military and economic targets, that attacking US forces will not remain without cost. This approach could lead to the formation of a dangerous cycle of attack and response; a cycle in which each military action pushes the other side toward a more severe reaction.
Meanwhile, the region's waters are gradually becoming one of the main arenas of competition. The importance of this issue is not limited to military operations. The security of shipping, energy transit, oil tankers, and trade routes are also directly affected by this confrontation.
In such an environment, Iran enjoys an important geographical advantage. The proximity of the operational theater to Iran's coasts means that Washington cannot separate the issue of protecting its naval forces from the geographical conditions of the region.
In contrast, the United States will try to neutralize this advantage by relying on its air and naval superiority and defense systems. For this reason, the battle between the two sides is not only a battle of missiles against ships; it is also a battle over the calculation of the costs and benefits of continued military presence.
If Iran can increase the cost and risk of the US military presence without needing to inflict direct and widespread damage, it will have achieved part of its deterrence objective. On the other hand, if the United States can continue to keep its carriers deployed in the region and simultaneously use them in military operations, Iran's effort to limit Washington's freedom of action will face greater difficulty.
Ultimately, the importance of the recent news should not be summarized merely as "whether the missiles hit the American ship or not." The real significance is that a US aircraft carrier, which is a symbol of Washington's power and military presence in distant regions, must now operate in an environment where the missile threat against it has become a serious variable in operational calculations.
This development could be one of the most important signs of a changing deterrence equation in the region; an equation in which military power is not measured only by the amount of weaponry, but also by each side's ability to impose costs, increase risk, and limit the other side's freedom of action.
In such circumstances, the future of the US carrier presence in the region will become more than ever a strategic issue; because as the cost of protecting these carriers increases, the question of the benefits of their continued presence will also become more serious for American decision-makers.
MNA

articles.title: Iran touts military response as US maintains blockade, hits tankers
articles.body:
Iran touts military response as US maintains blockade, hits tankers
Tehran says the time for proportionate retaliation is over after a US strike on Iranian tankers inside the blockade line.
Tehran, Iran – The United States continues to rely on a mix of military force and economic sanctions against Iran, which has so far only prompted authorities in Tehran to consider more forceful responses.
The US Central Command (CENTCOM) released video on Saturday showing three Iranian crude oil tankers being hit – one off Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub, another near Jask and a third in the Gulf of Oman. Two were “permanently disabled”, while a third sank after extensive bombing, CENTCOM said.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran President Pezeshkian calls for unity as US ramps up economic pressure
- list 2 of 3US says it hit Iran oil tankers accused of helping ‘regional proxies’
- list 3 of 3US, Iran engaged in tanker war: Where is the months-long conflict headed?
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later aired video of its own, showing explosives-laden projectiles crashing into multiple ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Aggressor US must know that it has no way but to leave the region and stop its malignance,” the IRGC said in a statement on Sunday. It added that a US-built sea drone was hit while trying to enter Iranian waters in the vital waterway, through which one fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes in peacetime.
The IRGC also said on Sunday it had fired several ballistic missiles towards a US aircraft carrier and another warship that are part of the network of vessels imposing the months-long naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports. Both vessels sustained some damage and fled, said the IRGC, although there was no immediate evidence of a successful hit and CENTCOM said the attacks were “evaded”.
The IRGC said it considered the acknowledgement by the US that missiles were launched towards its warships as “live evidence of the enemy’s strategic defeat and proof” of the force’s “offensive capabilities”.
Speaking during a private meeting of parliament members on Sunday, Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tehran has inflicted “significant blows” to US bases across the region to the “frustration” of leaders in Washington.
“The Americans have surely understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end and our recent strikes against aggressor bases was only a start,” said Ghalibaf, who is also Iran’s chief negotiator with the US.
Any further attacks against Iranian interests will be met with “faster, heavier and more painful” strikes from Iran, he warned.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the US attacks on Iranian ships illegal and a “war crime” that runs counter to the United Nations Charter.
Who is the blockade hurting?
US and Iranian officials provide different readings of what is transpiring after months of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the naval blockade imposed since mid-July.
The administration of President Donald Trump says more vessels have transited the strategically important waterway over recent weeks under US guidance, despite threats and attacks from Iran, with traffic allegedly nearing pre-war levels on some days. That account is countered by Iranian authorities, which say the strait remains closed.
The US military said about 90 commercial vessels have been redirected as part of the blockade, with several more disabled or boarded.
Crude oil exports from the Middle East during August were down 39 percent since the January and February baseline of 18.5 million barrels per day (mbpd), according to TankerTrackers. It said the current deficit is now 7.2mbpd, down from 12.4mbpd in May.
“Although most may recover in the coming months, Iran’s exports of 1.68mbpd (baseline number) may likely remain at zero for the foreseeable future; depending on any agreement,” the maritime intelligence company posted online on Sunday.
Iranian authorities have confirmed that they have been unable to get crude oil past the US warships imposing the blockade.
But they pointed out it does not equal a total halt to exports, with President Masoud Pezeshkian saying late last month that up to 90 million barrels of oil were exported during the brief period that the memorandum of understanding signed with the US in June was in effect.
Some of the oil is kept in floating storage outside the blockade, allowing Iran to gradually sell it at a discount to its main oil customer, China, despite US sanctions.
Washington is counting on those supplies running out in the foreseeable future.
“There’s probably only about 30 million barrels of Iranian crude oil left that China hasn’t bought,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday. “So that will run out soon and there will be no problem with China buying because they have no product.”
Bessent again hailed the “one-two punch” of the blockade and sanctions as part of what the Trump administration has branded Operation Economic Outcast, aimed at reducing Iran’s trade with neighbours and further isolating 90 million Iranians.
Iranian authorities have not said how much longer they expect to be able to sell oil amid the US onslaught, nor have they elaborated on whether they are exploring potential alternative routes.
But experts have said that while overland and rail routes can move limited refined products, fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gas towards Afghanistan, Iraq, Central Asia and beyond, they cannot offer a viable and scalable replacement for the volume transported by very large crude carriers through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Economy Ministry on Sunday established an “economic war headquarters” to counter the pressure, as the country deals with one of the world’s highest inflation rates, unemployment, energy imbalance and a host of other deep-seated issues.
But IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi suggested that the US was taking several times more economic damage from the war and blockade than Iran.
“If the US wants to deal one dollar in economic damage to Iran, it may deal several dollars’ worth of costs and damages to itself,” he said, pointing to lowered US strategic energy reserves and decreased aluminium exports from the region as examples.

articles.title: Romania issues air-raid alert amid Russian attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Romania issues air-raid alert amid Russian attack on Ukraine
The Romanian Ministry of National Defence reported this on Sunday, according to Ukrinform.
“On Saturday, September 5, at 23:40, the MoND’s radar surveillance system detected a group of aerial targets moving towards the river border with Ukraine,” the ministry said.
It added that Romania’s air defense systems were placed on combat alert.
“Two Spanish Air and Space Force F-18 aircraft and a Romanian Air Force IAR 330 Puma SOCAT helicopter were ready to scramble,” the military said.
The National Military Command Center notified the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations regarding the implementation of public alert measures for the northern part of Tulcea County.
A message was issued through the national RO-Alert system at 00:10.
After no violations of Romanian airspace were detected, the air-raid alert was lifted at 00:42.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine’s air defense forces neutralized 82 drones and six S8000 Banderol systems used by Russian forces to attack Ukraine overnight on September 6.
The Turkish Air Force deployed two F-16 fighter jets and support aircraft as part of NATO’s integrated air and missile defense activities in Romanian airspace.

articles.title: Report urges Britain to offer EU nuclear protection
articles.body:
Britain should explore what it calls a Deterrence Union with the European Union, formally extending its nuclear and conventional deterrent over the bloc in exchange for bespoke access to European defence funds, according to a report published by the Council on Geostrategy.
The paper, titled Towards a Hercules Hold: Maintaining a transatlantic defence industrial base, is written by Paul Mason and William Freer and carries a foreword by Tan Dhesi, the Labour MP for Slough and chair of the House of Commons Defence Committee.
Its central argument is that the transatlantic defence industrial base has begun to split, with Washington reprioritising resources towards hemispheric defence and countering China while the European Union deploys instruments such as the €150 billion SAFE facility in pursuit of strategic autonomy, and that those European mechanisms increasingly mandate the exclusion of third countries. Britain, sitting outside the European Union while maintaining deep security ties with Washington, is described as squeezed between two diverging defence giants and facing what the authors call a dangerous Hobson’s choice in capability standardisation.
The bridge has stopped working
The authors argue that the role Britain has traditionally assigned itself, acting as a transatlantic bridge, no longer serves the purpose it was designed for.
They write: “The historic approach of acting as a more passive transatlantic ‘bridge’ will prove insufficient to securing British interests. Instead, Britain should see itself as central to establishing a ‘Hercules hold’ to grip and sustain two diverging pillars. By focusing defence investment on select capabilities and championing interchangeability, HM Government can wield the influence necessary to maintain access to US technology while accelerating European rearmament.”
According to the report, further bifurcation risks cutting European allies off from cutting-edge American research and development along with North American surge capacity, leaving European nations with widening gaps in the high-end capabilities where the United States leads, among them ballistic missile defence, hypersonic strike and space systems, while integrated transatlantic defence firms face severe supply chain disruption.
What is being proposed
The Deterrence Union is the recommendation likely to attract most attention, since it would involve Britain formally offering nuclear protections to the European Union in return for deeper access to its defence market.
Alongside it the authors recommend championing hardware and munitions interchangeability across NATO, so that equipment can be physically swapped between allied platforms, and investing in a select portfolio of high-value technological chokepoints where British engineering becomes indispensable to both Washington and Brussels. They also call on the government formally to back the Canadian-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank as a source of non-exclusionary funding for transatlantic projects.
Interchangeability is the same concept the First Sea Lord set out in an interview published last month, describing it as going beyond interoperability so that it becomes agnostic which nation is conducting a given task, with allied navies acting for each other’s collective requirements and able to exchange capabilities.
Why the timing matters
The report lands as the American review of force posture in Europe gets under way. Elbridge Colby, the Under Secretary of War for Policy, told a meeting in Brussels last week that the review would examine the strategic posture of American forces on the continent even as Washington prioritises the Western Hemisphere and the First Island Chain, and confirmed that allies had been sent a written questionnaire seeking their views.
British access to European defence funding instruments has been under negotiation since 2024, and the SAFE facility in particular has been the subject of argument over the terms on which non-member states can participate.
Dhesi, who wrote the foreword, pressed the Prime Minister at Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday to commit to a pathway to three per cent of gross domestic product on defence by 2030, telling the Commons that Britain faces a significantly increased threat level and a United States leadership for which European security is no longer a priority.
The Council on Geostrategy is a London-based think tank founded in 2021 which focuses on British foreign and defence policy, the Indo-Pacific, and the maritime and technological dimensions of national strategy. Paul Mason is a journalist and author who co-presents the organisation’s Defence Talks podcast.

articles.title: Germany Unveils Anti-Sabotage Plan After Leipzig Airport Attack
articles.body:
Germany is preparing a comprehensive package of domestic security measures to counter Russian sabotage, cyberattacks, and hybrid threats following an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, Bild reported.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced that Berlin is planning robust countermeasures covering drone defense, the protection of critical infrastructure, cyber resilience, and enhanced surveillance to detect spies and potential terrorists.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russia’s hybrid attacks using explosive drones against airports, agents in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks, and sabotage of our infrastructure are a daily reality,” Dobrindt said. “These attacks will intensify, but we can fight back and defend ourselves.”
Under the proposal, Germany will expand the Federal Police’s mobile anti-drone capabilities. Rapid-reaction units equipped with specialized vehicles and helicopters will be stationed across nine key cities: Frankfurt am Main, Munich, Hamburg, Berlin, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Leipzig, Hanover, and Cologne.
Their operational remit will cover the protection of airspace over key transit hubs, airports, major railway stations, and the government quarter in Berlin, with the technical ability to intercept and neutralize explosive-laden drones.
The plan also grants critical infrastructure operators – including water utilities, energy companies, and defense manufacturing plants – expanded legal authority to actively counter and neutralize unauthorized drones without waiting for state law enforcement to arrive.
US Sanctions Chief Joins Moscow Talks as Putin Cites War Goals
Additionally, Berlin intends to deploy artificial intelligence tools, biometric facial recognition, and automated video surveillance at transport hubs to detect weapons, identify suspicious conduct, and track individuals suspected of espionage.
To guard against digital intrusion, Germany plans to establish a national “Cyberdome,” a distributed digital sensor network designed to detect and block coordinated cyberattacks.
Baltic shadow fleet pressure and rising sabotage wave
The domestic security initiative coincides with broader efforts by Berlin to apply economic and regulatory pressure against Moscow following the Aug. 4 drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Dobrindt publicly attributed responsibility for the airport attack directly to the Russian state, a stance endorsed across governing coalition parties. Siemtje Möller, foreign policy spokesperson for the Social Democratic Party (SPD) parliamentary group, affirmed that directly naming Russia was the correct course of action.
According to the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ), German authorities are evaluating punitive measures targeting Russia’s maritime “shadow fleet” in the Baltic Sea. Officials are exploring stricter administrative, inspection, and legal mechanisms to impede or halt the transit of tankers used by Moscow to circumvent international sanctions.
The heightened security alerts follow a confidential assessment by Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), which recorded 165 suspected sabotage cases, 24 espionage investigations, and 747 suspicious drone flights nationwide during the first eight months of 2026.

articles.title: "Flash" warned of possible massive Russian strikes on Kyiv in winter
articles.body:
"Flash" warned of possible massive Russian strikes on Kyiv in winter
Kyiv • UNN
Serhii Beskrestnov predicts massive Russian strikes on Kyiv's systems this winter. He called for considering the evacuation of civilians and warned of a shortage of Patriots.
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, adviser to the President of Ukraine on defense technologies, warned of the risk of massive Russian strikes on Kyiv’s energy, water-supply and heating infrastructure. The Guardian reports this, UNN reports.
Details
According to the publication, Beskrestnov said that Russia and Ukraine had found themselves in an “escalation of a war of long-range strikes with a growing risk to civilians, in which neither side can achieve a complete victory.”
The official also expressed concern about Kyiv’s prospects this winter and noted that the city authorities should consider evacuating civilians, particularly elderly people, in advance.
This is now a war of cities, a war of infrastructure. No one wins this war, because after the war both countries will have destroyed their economies and infrastructure. So this is foolishness. We must stop this war. We proposed that Russia stop this war, but Russia does not want to stop
According to “Flash,” Russia may carry out sustained bombardments of Kyiv’s electricity, water-supply and heating systems this winter using high-speed ballistic missiles, which it is producing at a rate of more than 100 per month.
Earlier this week, Vladimir Putin said that the Russian military had been “ordered to prepare and carry out massive strikes” against Ukraine’s energy facilities, showing no signs of ending the war
It is horrifying to me. We are talking about 2–3 million people, and Russia understands that this could create a catastrophe in Kyiv
According to the publication, Ukraine is critically short of American Patriot interceptor missiles, the main weapon capable of stopping ballistic missiles. At the same time, according to available information, Beskrestnov said that he was “not sure” that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy would be able to obtain enough from abroad to prevent a crisis.
We remind you
Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Russia is intensifying its strikes and preparing for winter. He explained that Russian attacks on Ukrainian logistics were one of the reasons for Ukraine’s strikes on the respective facilities in the russian federation.

articles.title: Drones Attack Sanctioned Russian Vessel Lady Maria in Mediterranean Sea
articles.body:
Drones attacked the sanctioned vessel Lady Maria in the Mediterranean Sea, which is reportedly used to transport Russian weapons.
The NEVZOROV Telegram channel published footage of the attack.
The vessel was targeted by drones equipped with a system for dropping munitions. The strikes caused a small fire to break out on board.
According to data from the MarineTraffic vessel-tracking service, the ship departed the Algerian port of Oran and was headed for an undisclosed destination.
The latest route updates indicate that the vessel was sailing through the Mediterranean Sea, passing near the island of Crete on its way toward Syria.
The vessel Lady Maria (IMO 9220641) is currently under U.S. OFAC sanctions under the name STELLA-MARIA. The vessel has been linked to the Russian company MG-FLOT LLC (formerly TransMorFlot LLC) under the sanctions regime established by Executive Order 14024.
In addition to the United States, Ukraine also imposed sanctions on the vessel on May 23, 2026. The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) stated that Lady Maria is involved in transporting military cargo and weapons for Russia.
According to intelligence reports, the vessel has been used on the Novorossiysk–Tartus route. It has also been linked to the transportation of weapons from Syria to Russia.
Other vessels operated by MG-FLOT LLC are also subject to sanctions. The company’s vessels have likewise been used to transport ammunition from North Korea.
There is currently no confirmed information on whether the drones were Ukrainian. However, the activity of Ukrainian intelligence and security services in these waters is not new.
In May 2026, Greek fishermen found a Ukrainian Magura naval drone near the southern part of Lefkada, an island in the Ionian Sea in western Greece.
In December 2025, the Security Service of Ukraine struck a tanker belonging to Russia’s shadow fleet in the neutral waters of the Mediterranean Sea for the first time.
Moreover, given that the vessel has been used to transport weapons to Syria, an Israeli strike cannot be ruled out. Israel has previously carried out attacks on Iranian ports, including Bandar-e Anzali on the Caspian Sea.

articles.title: Ukraine, NATO Chief Discuss Air Defense Ahead of Ramstein Meeting
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara held a telephone conversation with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte to discuss preparations for the upcoming Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting in the “Ramstein” format, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry announced on Saturday evening, Sept. 5.
During the call, Khmara and Rutte reviewed Ukraine’s priority battlefield needs, focusing primarily on securing additional air defense systems and expanding financial contributions for the Defense Forces.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Khmara characterized partner support across these two domains as Ukraine’s primary objective ahead of the multilateral summit scheduled for the coming days.
Khmara emphasized the necessity of consolidated allied assistance in strengthening air defenses, stating that Kyiv is counting on continued partner unity and swift decision-making.
He highlighted the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) program, which facilitates the targeted procurement and delivery of critical armaments to Ukrainian forces.
The discussions with NATO leadership follow a separate phone call between Khmara and German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Friday, in which both officials coordinated preparations for next week’s Ramstein gathering.
The previous Contact Group meeting occurred on June 18 at NATO headquarters in Brussels, co-chaired by the UK and Germany.
Urgent Patriot missile requests
The consultations ahead of the Ramstein summit follow a request by Kyiv urging the European Commission to allocate several billion euros from the EU’s €90 billion ($105 billion) support loan to purchase PAC-3 Patriot interceptor missiles.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 5, 2026
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced Ukraine’s request on Sept. 2 in Brussels prior to a meeting with Rutte, confirming that member states are actively reviewing the proposal.
The requested funds are intended to finance high-end air defense capabilities, particularly PAC-3 missiles, which serve as Ukraine’s primary countermeasure against Russian ballistic missile strikes.
The EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan has already disbursed €8.5 billion (roughly $9.9 billion) since June to finance drone and missile manufacturing, alongside procurement plans for European-built fighter jets.
Concurrently, the EU and Ukraine are advancing the “Freyja” project, an initiative aimed at jointly developing a European anti-ballistic missile defense system.
Kyiv’s air defense push follows Khmara’s address to EU defense ministers on Sept. 1, where he outlined pressing operational gaps. In response, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas acknowledged that interceptors are in short supply, urging member states to review existing stockpiles and consider transferring or selling Patriot missiles approaching the end of their operational service lives.

articles.title: Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns
articles.body:
Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, Leon Panetta, the former US defense secretary, has warned, as the US president struggles to find his way out of the controversial conflict.
Panetta declared in an interview that the war with Iran – launched by Trump over six months ago – risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight.
“It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama, suggesting the conflict is on course to become “another failed war” in the Middle East “like Iraq and Afghanistan”.
“I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added.
Panetta spoke to the Guardian days after the US army secretary, Dan Driscoll, abruptly resigned, departing amid the conflict, following reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over a series of firings.
US service members “are going to war at a time when there’s tremendous turmoil at the Pentagon, in the command structure, which really creates a sense that there’s nobody in charge”, Panetta, who served as defense secretary from 2011 to 2013, added. “And I just think that, whether it’s Iran, or whether it’s our adversaries, they’re now looking at the United States, and see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country.”
He said: “My biggest concern right now is we live in a very dangerous world, with the primary threats coming from China, from Russia, from North Korea, and from terrorism, and yes, from Iran as well. But what I’m concerned about is that we’re sending a message of weakness to our primary adversaries.
“And while they continue to meet and support each other in this axis that’s been created, I think they look at the United States as being particularly weak right now, and that’s a horrible message to send at a time when we’re facing those kinds of threats.”
In a statement, the Pentagon insisted it was “firing on all cylinders” under Hegseth’s leadership.
“The premise that the Department is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation,” the chief Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said. “This is what reform looks like.”
The White House was also contacted for comment.
In March, just three weeks after the US and Israel launched their military operation in Iran, Panetta told the Guardian he believed Trump was stuck between a “rock and a hard place” as he weighed whether to expand the war in a bid to eliminate Iran’s leverage over the strait of Hormuz, or “just simply walk away and declare victory”, despite the risk of perceived failure.
Earlier this week Panetta said he “absolutely” believed Trump remains in that position. “He’s boxed himself in,” he said.
Trump now has three options, according to Panetta. The first would be to walk away and “admit that it’s a failed war”, something Panetta finds it difficult to see Trump doing.
The second would be to draw out the current “stalemate, with periodic attacks going back and forth, tit for tat”, and both sides attempting to “avoid the startup of a more dangerous war” while refusing to either negotiate or surrender.
That approach, Panetta believes, would produce “what all parties feared”: another protracted war in the Middle East.
The third option, he said, would be for the US to take control of the strait of Hormuz, and remove Iran’s “most dangerous leverage point” over the US, “which is the ability … to close and disrupt” the global trade chokepoint.
“So the president either steps up and does what’s necessary to open up the strait of Hormuz, or, as I said, he just continues to play … this game of pretending that somehow he’s winning a stalemate when the fact is he’s not,” Panetta said.
Asked if he believed the war is “winnable” for the US, Panetta replied: “It’s only winnable if there is a dramatic change in the attitude of the United States that makes clear that the objective, the primary objective by the United States at this point in time, is to reopen the strait of Hormuz.”
He also argued that Trump has damaged his credibility by repeatedly erroneously claiming that a deal to end the war is imminent, and that the strait of Hormuz is open.
“So the real question is, is he going to make a decision to actually deliver?” Panetta asked. “For a lot of reasons, right now, he’s caught in the worst of every world because not only does he not have credibility, but any threats he makes are totally ignored.”
Earlier this week, JD Vance told reporters that he would not describe the current military conflict with Iran as a “war”. And asked whether he expected the conflict to be over by November’s US midterm elections, the vice-president replied: “I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.”
Panetta told the Guardian he believes many Americans have “lost faith” in Trump’s “ability to handle this war”, pointing to recent polling that he said found that a majority of Americans believe that conflict with Iran was a mistake and are against it.
He also said he hopes the Pentagon and Trump’s broader administration learn from what happened with the extremely long deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, which arrived in Thailand this week after a record-breaking deployment supporting US operations against Iran that lasted more than 260 days without a port visit, amid reports of deteriorating living conditions and mental health aboard.
“Bottom line is, you do not deploy people endlessly into a war zone without making some kind of plans for rotation,” Panetta said.
“So it’s not just that the war is going badly – I think there’s also kind of a lack of trust in our military as to whether or not they are properly supporting our men and women who are putting their lives on the line.”

articles.title: US Destroys 3 Iranian Tankers After Warships Attacked in Gulf
articles.body:
The US military struck and disabled three crude oil tankers operated by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) after Iranian forces launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy warships patrolling regional waters.
According to a statement released by US Central Command (CENTCOM) on X, an American aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer “evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks,” with no US personnel injured and no damage reported to the naval vessels.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In immediate retaliation, US forces conducted precision strikes against three IRGC-linked vessels. CENTCOM reported that American strikes permanently disabled the crude oil tanker M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near the port of Jask.
A third vessel, the unladen tanker M/T Kylo (also known as Noxen), was struck in multiple critical areas in the Gulf of Oman and subsequently sank, which CENTCOM later confirmed through released video footage.
“The three Iranian crude oil tankers are part of a multi-billion dollar illicit shadow network that finances the IRGC and its regional proxies,” CENTCOM stated. “Iran has no means to protect them.”
Thanks to the precision and professionalism of American service members, the M/T Kylo sank in the Gulf of Oman today and joined Iran’s navy at the bottom of the sea. pic.twitter.com/OwSDMl8SSQ
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) September 6, 2026
Following the strikes, the IRGC announced that it targeted six vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, claiming the group included three ships linked to the US and three commercial oil tankers.
According to Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency, the IRGC characterized the operation as retaliation for the US strikes on its tankers, alleging the commercial vessels had navigated through “unauthorized routes.”
US Envoys Hold 3-Hour Kremlin Talks With Putin
Iranian military authorities subsequently issued warnings to maritime traffic across the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, ordering vessels to avoid lanes not sanctioned by Tehran.
Escalation risks and threats to European bases
The direct exchange of fire marks a significant escalation in maritime hostilities amid stalled diplomatic negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz shipping corridor.
The maritime clashes follow warnings from Iranian regime insiders that Tehran has considered expanding its retaliatory targets beyond the Middle East to include US military assets in southeastern Europe and Cyprus.
Insiders previously indicated that Iranian commanders evaluated potential strikes against facilities such as Bulgaria’s Bezmer air base – which approved refueling operations for US aircraft – and the British sovereign base at RAF Akrotiri on Cyprus, which was struck by an explosive drone in March.
Iranian planners have also examined targeting subsea fiber-optic cables traversing the Strait of Hormuz if hostilities continue to intensify.
The threats coincided with statements from US President Donald Trump warning that Washington would target Iranian domestic infrastructure, declaring the US would destroy a bridge or power plant in Iran every time Tehran attacks a ship navigating the strait.
While defense analysts note that Iranian medium-range ballistic missiles face accuracy limitations at extended ranges, Tehran’s rhetoric has grown uncompromising.
The appointment of hardline former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei as Iran’s top security official has underscored Tehran’s willingness to absorb higher risks and impose broader economic and military costs on Washington and its allies amid the breakdown of maritime transit talks.

articles.title: Ukraine put its own peace proposals on the table as two US envoys reached Kyiv for the first time
articles.body:
After a months-long pause, US President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner opened their first round of peace talks in Kyiv to end the Russo-Ukrainian war. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced their visit and talks on Telegram on 6 September. A day earlier, they visited Moscow and met with Russian President Vladimir Putin there. Ukraine came in with prepared proposals and a demand for security guarantees. Witkoff called the discussion substantive, and the British, French, and German national security advisers joined the later rounds. Despite their previous multiple visits to Moscow, this was their first-ever visit to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy came with a written package and one demand
Zelenskyy gathered his negotiating team before the meeting and wrote on Telegram that Ukraine was ready to talk.
"Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A dignified character of the post-war peace is needed. Our proposals have been prepared," he said, adding that it was important to work in a coordinated, substantive, and realistic way.
The preparatory meeting brought together head of the President's Office Kyrylo Budanov, Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umierov, Servant of the People faction leader David Arakhamia, and First Deputy Head of the President's Office Serhii Kyslytsia—Ukraine's likely negotiating team.
The post announcing the start of the talks, published shortly after 2 p.m., carried video of Zelenskyy greeting the two Americans. He also told reporters the day would run in stages: one session with the US side, then another with the European advisers. After the first part, Zelenskyy thanked American and European partners.
The presidential website had published no report on the talks by the time this article went out.
Ending the fighting is not the goal, the envoys said
Witkoff called the talks substantive and said the US team was ready to continue working, TSN reported. He said Washington was looking for openings on external security issues and coordinating closely with Germany, France, and the UK.
Kushner said the goal was not only to end the fighting but to create conditions for a lasting peace. He called it “a very, very hard and complex problem,” but “a very worthy problem of solving,” and said a lasting peace should allow Ukraine to turn its wartime “bravery and ingenuity and strength” toward rebuilding the country.
Kushner also said Trump is determined to end the war and then shift toward investment and economic cooperation, which he argued could bring the countries closer and open new opportunities for Ukraine and Europe. He added that the talks continue between visits, with the US side speaking almost daily with the four Ukrainian negotiators, whom he named only by their first names.
Ukraine logged impacts at 11 sites while the American peace delegation was still in Moscow
The Europeans joined the later rounds
Zelenskyy's spokesman Serhii Nykyforov said the first round with Witkoff and Kushner had finished, and that a second, expanded round with the national security advisers of the UK, France, and Germany would follow after a short break. A source familiar with the matter told Reuters the three advisers were in Kyiv on Sunday, without specifying which sessions they would attend.
A third round then opened, public broadcaster Suspilne reported. Witkoff described the discussion as substantive, concrete, and important shortly before it started.
Moscow, the day before
Trending Now
Witkoff and Kushner held three hours of talks with Putin in Moscow on 5 September. Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov stated the meeting was substantive, very frank, and constructive, and said Putin told them Russia would achieve its war aims and that the war's so-called "root causes" must be removed—Kremlin shorthand for Ukraine abandoning NATO membership and disarming, which Kyiv rejects.
Ukraine orders temporary ceasefire as US envoys visit Moscow. Air raid alert sounds in Kyiv immediately as pause begins
A White House representative told Radio Svoboda that the sides discussed concrete plans for next steps, to be announced in the coming weeks. Bloomberg reported that sources close to the Kremlin said Putin is ready to end the war only on his own terms, with Moscow's demands hardening. Axios reported that a US Treasury official responsible for sanctions policy joined the trip but did not attend the Putin meeting, alongside State Department and National Security Council staff.
Trump said on 4 September that Witkoff and Kushner were carrying a proposal to both Moscow and Kyiv, which he described as fresh, without giving details.
How the envoys reached Kyiv
Umierov published video this morning showing Budanov, Umierov, Arakhamia, and Kyslytsia welcoming Witkoff and Kushner at Kyiv’s railway station as the US envoys arrived for talks.
Ukraine had prepared to receive the envoys by air, but Russian strikes made that impossible, Zelenskyy said. He met them instead on Sofiivska Square before the delegation went inside St Sophia's Cathedral. In a 4 September address, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would keep Russian airspace safe for the envoys’ travel and demanded Moscow do the same.
A pause that covered two capitals
Ukraine ordered a three-day halt to strikes on Moscow around the visit, and the Kremlin claimed it would pause strikes on Kyiv until Monday. Nothing else stopped. Ukraine logged impacts at 11 sites across the country while the American delegation was in the Russian capital. Ukraine's 6 September strike hit the Ryazan oil refinery and set a core unit on fire, about 470 km from Ukraine.
Witkoff and Kushner to visit Kyiv and Moscow to revive peace talks as Russia ramps up attacks across Ukraine
Twenty months of rounds without a deal
Trump made ending Russia’s war a priority after taking office in January 2025, but US-mediated talks produced little and later stalled during the US-Israeli war against Iran. Washington said in early August it intended to step up the effort, and Russian attacks intensifying pushed a planned August visit to Kyiv back.
The visit was confirmed on 4 September, after two weeks of heavy Russian attacks on Kyiv, including a drone strike on the headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and an earlier six-day bombardment. Previous talks also left Kyiv and Moscow far apart over Donbas, where Russia demands Ukrainian withdrawal from fortified cities still under Kyiv’s control.

articles.title: Turkey pushes KAAN stealth jet as tensions with Israel deepen
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey pushes KAAN stealth jet as tensions with Israel deepen
Turkey is accelerating development of its fifth-generation KAAN fighter jet as Ankara seeks greater military independence amid increasingly open tensions with Israel and Israeli strikes targeting potential Turkish military expansion in Syria.
The Turkish-built fighter is intended eventually to provide Ankara with a sovereign alternative to the US-made F-35, a programme Turkey was expelled from after acquiring Russia's S-400 air defence system.
Turkey had been a partner in the F-35 programme and planned to operate the stealth fighter before Washington removed Ankara and later imposed sanctions over the S-400 purchase.
The setback left Turkey without an operational fifth-generation fighter, while Israel operates the F-35I Adir, giving it a significant advantage in stealth air power.
KAAN, developed by Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAS), is intended to narrow that gap while reducing Ankara's dependence on foreign suppliers for advanced military capabilities.
The aircraft's first prototype flew in February 2024, while a newer prototype began taxi tests in July as Turkey moves towards a more advanced phase of testing.
Turkish officials say the aircraft was designed domestically from the ground up as part of a decades-long effort to establish an independent combat aircraft industry.
KAAN is being developed with stealth, internal weapons carriage, advanced radar, electronic warfare and sensor fusion.
These technologies intend to make the aircraft harder to detect and allow pilots to combine information from multiple sensors into a single battlefield picture.
However, one of the programme's biggest remaining challenges is the engine.
KAAN's prototypes and initial production aircraft rely on US-made General Electric F110 engines.
Turkey is developing the TF35000, a domestic 35,000-pound-thrust-class engine intended eventually to power KAAN, but Turkish Aerospace has indicated that integration is targeted for around 2032.
Developing an advanced fighter engine is particularly difficult because it requires technologies including heat-resistant alloys, turbine cooling, precision manufacturing and sophisticated digital controls.
Until Turkey succeeds, KAAN will reduce some forms of foreign dependence while retaining another through its reliance on US propulsion.
Israeli aggression raises the stakes
That vulnerability has become more significant as relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated.
Syria has emerged as a major arena of tension since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 and the emergence of a new government closely aligned with Ankara.
In April 2025, Israel struck the T4, Palmyra and Hama airbases after Turkish military teams had inspected the facilities as Ankara considered expanding its military presence in Syria.
Sources told Reuters at the time that the attack rendered T4 effectively unusable, with one regional intelligence official describing the strikes as a message that Israel would not accept an expanded Turkish presence.
Tensions escalated further in August, when Israel bombed the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northwestern Syria after claiming Turkish troops were preparing to deploy there.
Turkey and Syria denied that any permanent Turkish deployment was planned.
US envoy Tom Barrack later said US intelligence had examined the Israeli claim and concluded that Turkey was not moving military assets into the base.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has nevertheless warned that Israel would not tolerate an expanding Turkish military presence in Syria.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has also warned President Recep Tayyip Erdogan against what he described as "dangerous" military moves in Syria and against testing Israel's willingness to act.
Israel has also opposed Turkey regaining access to the F-35.
Netanyahu said in July that he opposed a possible US sale of the aircraft to Ankara, arguing that it could alter the regional balance of power.
President Donald Trump has signalled a willingness to reconsider Turkey's access to the F-35, although political and legal obstacles remain.
For Ankara, Israel's fifth-generation air advantage, its strikes on Syrian military infrastructure linked to possible Turkish deployments and its opposition to Turkey acquiring F-35s add further strategic importance to KAAN.
A mature KAAN equipped with a Turkish engine, radar, electronic warfare systems and weapons would give Ankara a degree of independent high-end air power it currently lacks.
Israel, however, already operates a mature and combat-tested F-35 fleet, while KAAN remains in development.
Turkey is also seeking foreign partners for the programme, with Saudi Arabia in advanced discussions over possible involvement.
If Ankara succeeds in combining KAAN with a domestically produced engine and indigenous combat systems, the fighter could significantly reduce Turkey's reliance on Washington while beginning to narrow one of Israel's most important technological advantages over it.

articles.title: Trump official says ‘there may not be a nuclear agreement’ with Iran
articles.body:
Trump official says ‘there may not be a nuclear agreement’ with Iran
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright’s comments could signal that US hopes for a nuclear deal are dimming.
As the United States and Iran resume trading attacks, a top US official has publicly downplayed the chances of one of President Donald Trump’s initial key objectives in the US and Israel’s war on Iran: getting a signed nuclear agreement.
During an interview on Sunday with US channel ABC News, the US Energy Secretary, Chris Wright, said “there may not” be a nuclear deal, signalling that the US may pivot instead to launching strikes against any Iranian efforts to build nuclear infrastructure.
Recommended Stories
