articles.title: Soviet-era rifle still beats Russia’s newest AK-12, analysis shows
articles.body:
- A Ukrainian gunsmith examined five captured Russian rifles and found barrel defects in all three AK-12 generations, including one nearly unfired 2026-made model.
- He said two Soviet-era AK-74 rifles, despite decades of heavy use and poor maintenance, held up better internally than the newer AK-12 samples.
A Ukrainian gunsmith who services captured Russian assault rifles for Ukrainian troops says the newest generation of Kalashnikov rifle, the AK-12, consistently shows worse barrel quality than the decades-old AK-74 it was meant to replace, based on a detailed inspection of five trophy weapons spanning more than 40 years of production.
Dmytro, who runs a weapons service channel called OrkovNetMedia, opened the video by noting that Ukrainian law allows soldiers to legally declare captured firearms, including rifles still configured for automatic fire, a policy he called “maximally civilized.” He said five declared trophy rifles arrived at his shop on a single day. Under Ukrainian law, owners of declared trophy weapons cannot convert them to civilian semi-automatic configuration or otherwise modify them until martial law ends. Each rifle must be kept, registered and inspected in the same condition it was captured.
For the inspection, Dmytro laid out three AK-12 rifles representing three separate production generations, alongside two AK-74 rifles serving as comparison points. He used a borescope, a thin camera on a flexible or rigid cable, to examine the inside of each barrel without disassembly, and said the tool costs only a few thousand hryvnia. He argued every soldier picking up a battlefield rifle should carry one, since a weapon’s exterior condition tells a buyer almost nothing about the state of its bore, and he has had soldiers arrive at his shop disappointed after hauling a 15 to 20 kilogram rifle out of the field only to learn its barrel was ruined.
The first rifle he examined was a first-generation AK-12 from 2019, already seven years old. He said its bore had clearly suffered from prolonged exposure to poor conditions, describing a foul-smelling residue inside consistent with organic decay near where the rifle had lain in the field. Despite that, once cleaned, the barrel’s overall condition along its length was reasonable, with chrome damage concentrated mainly at the muzzle crown, the precisely machined edge at the barrel’s opening that governs accuracy, rather than throughout the bore. Dmytro said damage limited to the crown, while still a defect, would only modestly affect the rifle’s grouping at typical combat ranges and would not be considered disqualifying.
The second rifle, a second-generation AK-12, arrived in comparatively better external condition, having spent limited time in the field rather than in long-term storage. Under the borescope, however, Dmytro found the bore’s chrome plating had already begun flaking away, and he described the muzzle crown as looking “like beavers had gnawed it,” calling the damage worse than what he found in either the older first-generation model or, notably, in a much older AK-74. He concluded the rifle offered no real advantage over an unusable weapon and recommended discarding it outright, joking that its only remaining use was as a cleaning-rod holder.
The most striking rifle in the video was a third-generation AK-12 manufactured in 2026 and captured in what Dmytro said was nearly unfired condition. He said the weapon had belonged to a Russian soldier identified only as Yemelyanov, who was killed while still holding the rifle in a firm grip, having reportedly used it for roughly one week before his death. The rifle’s cleaning rod remained in place, unused, a detail Dmytro cited as further evidence the weapon had seen almost no service. Externally and even partway into the bore, the rifle looked close to new. Deeper inspection near the gas port, however, revealed what he described as pitted cavities in the metal, comparing the damage to the progression of a perforating ulcer, which he warned could eventually develop into holes straight through the barrel wall. The muzzle crown was also poorly formed despite the rifle’s minimal use. Dmytro’s verdict was that the rifle, brand new and nearly unfired, was still not worth carrying into combat and was suitable only as a keepsake.
By contrast, an AK-74 manufactured in 1983, shown as a comparison baseline, displayed an extremely high round count and had reportedly spent roughly 90% of its service life without proper maintenance. Despite that history, Dmytro said the bore remained in what he called a “living” condition along its full length, with a clean muzzle crown and no chrome damage of the kind he found in the newer rifles. A second AK-74 from 1990, shown briefly afterward, had heavier external rust and a dirtier muzzle assembly, and Dmytro admitted he had expected it to be in better shape than it was, but its bore still showed less wear than the AK-12 samples and its chamber remained undamaged.
Beyond barrel condition, Dmytro flagged a specific mechanical failure he said he has traced to at least one Russian soldier’s death. He described a small part on early AK-12 rifles known as the two-round-burst limiter, made, in his assessment, from substandard metal that can jam and lock the bolt in the rearward position. He said he had been told secondhand that a Russian soldier whose rifle jammed in this way during combat was unable to clear it and was killed shortly afterward, with the disabled rifle later brought to him for inspection.
Dmytro closed the review with a broader assessment based on his repeated experience servicing trophy weapons, cautioning it reflected his personal opinion rather than a formal engineering study. He said that, counterintuitively, older AK-12 production batches have tended to have better barrels than newer ones, citing several AK-12K carbines he had separately inspected, most of which he judged to be poor quality. He argued the AK-74 remains easier to maintain and modify in the field, since components like muzzle devices and barrel liners can be swapped in minutes, while equivalent parts on the AK-12, including its safety selector, are often pinned or swaged in place and effectively impossible to remove despite factory documentation suggesting otherwise. His overall conclusion was that the original AK-74 was built for military durability, while today’s Kalashnikov-brand rifles, in his view, are built primarily to win state procurement contracts rather than to withstand sustained combat use.
Reports of manufacturing defects have followed the AK-12 since its earliest development. Russian arms testing officials publicly acknowledged unspecified “technical faults” during the rifle’s 2012 preliminary trials without disclosing details, and Kalashnikov Concern scrapped that original design entirely in 2016, rebuilding the rifle around the AK-400 prototype to address the Russian military’s concerns over cost and reliability in automatic fire before adopting the redesigned version as today’s AK-12.

articles.title: Qalibaf warns of faster, heavier Iranian response to any new aggression
articles.body:
Qalibaf warns of faster, heavier Iranian response to any new aggression
TEHRAN — Iran will respond to any new aggression against its national interests and security with a faster, heavier, and more painful response, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Sunday, warning that the era of “proportionate responses” had come to an end.
Addressing an open session of parliament, Qalibaf said the United States should understand that “the rules of the game have changed” and that Iran’s recent strikes against hostile US positions were only the beginning.
“Any aggression against Iran’s national interests will be met with a faster, heavier and more painful response,” he said.
Qalibaf also stated that recent Iranian military strikes against US installations had confused American leaders, accusing Washington of resorting to 'deceptive tactics,' including the use of artificial intelligence to generate fabricated battlefield footage.
The speaker thanked the Iranian public for enduring two “imposed wars” involving the United States and Israel, referring to the 12-day and 40-day conflicts. He said maintaining domestic cohesion and strengthening external deterrence were essential to confronting external threats.
“Any speech or action that weakens these two fundamental pillars is contrary to rational prudence,” Qalibaf said, urging officials to avoid moves that could undermine national unity.
Turning to the economic front, Qalibaf said Iran must respond to intensified sanctions by strengthening domestic production, improving management of imports and supply chains, protecting energy infrastructure and making greater use of the country’s technical and professional expertise.
He also called on the government to improve the quality of public services and move more quickly to address economic difficulties, saying that while Iranians were prepared to endure hardship in confronting the “terrorist US government,” they would not accept mismanagement or inaction.
“The people expect us to manage the current situation properly and swiftly,” he said, describing this as their “indisputable and inalienable right.”

articles.title: Propaganda and military training are being intensified in Russian schools
articles.body:
Propaganda and military training are being intensified in Russian schools
Kyiv • UNN
In particular, social studies and foreign languages have been reduced, while the teaching of history based on Medinsky’s textbooks, military training, and propaganda of "traditional values" have been intensified.
In the new academic year, propaganda has been intensified in Russian schools. Children have had their study of social studies reduced to free up classroom hours for history and military training, and schools have also introduced subjects about "traditional values." This is reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
The new academic year in Russian schools has brought seven new or updated propaganda initiatives—nearly three times more than last year. One of the main changes is the further reduction of social studies. It will be removed from the eighth grade, and the freed-up hours will be given to history. This means less time for law, economics, politics, and the work of state institutions—knowledge that helps schoolchildren understand society and critically assess the authorities’ decisions
Instead, according to available data, eighth- and ninth-grade students will study from unified history textbooks prepared with the participation of Putin’s propagandist Medinsky. They will devote even more attention to the confrontation with the West, "traditional values," and the war, while in ninth grade the school year in history will begin with lessons on "Russia—our sacred state."
In grades 5–7, foreign-language instruction will be reduced from three lessons per week to two. At the same time, fifth-graders will be given "Spiritual and Moral Culture of Russia" in the second semester. The subject is intended to shape "traditional values" through the study of state officials and military personnel, primarily participants in the war against Ukraine. The military component is also being strengthened. "Fundamentals of Life Safety and Defense of the Fatherland" will be divided into two compulsory courses—life safety and basic military training—with 34 hours each. Schools are also introducing grades for behavior and a new concept of historical education, which is intended to raise "patriotically minded "youth"
These changes continue the Kremlin’s policy toward school education, which intensified after the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. At that time, schools introduced "Conversations About Important Things," flag-raising ceremonies, the "Movement of the First," new history textbooks, military training, and advisers to school principals for educational work.
Last year, social studies was already removed from grades 6–7. Now it is being reduced by another year, freeing up time for "history," military training, and state ideology

russia is introducing military training, propaganda, and drone-operation instruction in the occupied territories of Ukraine. Cadet classes are planned from 2026.

articles.title: Trump Envoys Hold Three-Hour Talks With Putin in Moscow Ahead of Kyiv Visit
articles.body:

Trump Envoys Hold Three-Hour Talks With Putin in Moscow Ahead of Kyiv Visit
US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held more than three hours of talks with Russian leader Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Reuters on September 6, a White House official described the meeting as “substantive” and said further information on the next steps would be announced in the coming weeks. Putin’s aide Yuri Ushakov separately characterized the talks as “substantive, constructive, and extremely frank.”
The meeting lasted three hours and 10 minutes and focused primarily on possible approaches to ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
During the meeting, Witkoff told Putin, “When we retire, we’ll have all these incredible stories and memories, and yours will be right at the top of it all.”
Ushakov said the US delegation arrived with a number of proposals concerning a potential settlement and that Witkoff and Kushner would take Moscow’s position into account during their subsequent contacts in Kyiv.
“The US representatives seriously prepared for the trip to Moscow, they formulated a whole range of considerations regarding ways of settlement,” Ushakov said. He also said contacts between Trump and Putin would continue alongside diplomatic work involving Witkoff and Kushner.
“Putin and Trump will maintain personal contacts, and work through Witkoff and Kushner will also continue,” Ushakov said. The discussions extended beyond Ukraine, according to Ushakov, and included potential large-scale US-Russian economic projects.
After leaving Moscow, the aircraft carrying Witkoff and Kushner landed in Rzeszów, Poland. The US envoys are expected to travel to Kyiv for talks with Ukrainian officials on September 6.
Their Moscow visit took place amid a temporary arrangement concerning strikes on cities involved in the diplomatic process. On September 5, the Kremlin said Putin had ordered Russian forces not to strike Kyiv for three days beginning at midnight.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, following contacts with the US representatives, said Ukraine was also prepared to observe a temporary halt to aerial strikes involving cities connected to the negotiations.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills two people in Gaza, medics say
articles.body:
Israeli strike kills two people in Gaza, medics say
CAIRO, Sept 6 - An Israeli strike killed at least two Palestinians, including a child, in the Gaza Strip on Sunday, health officials said.
Mohamed Abu Selmia, head of the enclave's largest Al Shifa Hospital, said the Israeli airstrike struck a vehicle in western Gaza City killing two people, including a girl, and wounding six others.
The Israeli military did not immediately comment on the incident.
An October 2025 U.S.-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the territory, but it failed to end strikes by the Israeli military, which it said aimed to thwart attacks by Hamas and other Gaza militants.
Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement U.S. President Donald Trump's broader plan to end the Gaza conflict, which also includes Israeli withdrawals and Hamas disarmament.
More than 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect last October, according to the territory's health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Hamas does not usually disclose information about fatalities among its fighters. REUTERS

articles.title: Iran establishes ‘economic war headquarters’ amid US conflict, sanctions
articles.body:
Sahin Demir
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
Iran’s Economy Ministry has established an “economic war headquarters” to coordinate and accelerate responses to economic problems arising from wartime conditions, Deputy Economy Minister Morteza Zamanian said Sunday.
Zamanian told the Tasnim news agency that the body would initially focus on issues falling within the ministry’s responsibilities and authorities.
He said it would seek to quickly address war-related problems affecting businesses, trade, financing and other areas of the economy.
For issues extending beyond the ministry’s authority, Zamanian said the ministry would use its role in broader economic policymaking, including through the government’s economic commission and economic headquarters, to coordinate among institutions and pursue solutions at higher levels.
The main function of the new body is to centrally identify disruptions caused by wartime conditions and develop practical solutions, he said.
Zamanian added that the mechanism is intended to prevent issues requiring cooperation among several government agencies from becoming stalled by bureaucracy.
Measures being pursued include tax and customs support, banking facilities and financial instruments for businesses affected by the conflict, he said.
The move comes amid an ongoing conflict that began when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February, followed by Iranian retaliatory attacks against US targets across the region.
Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in June, mediated by Pakistan and Qatar, outlining steps toward ending hostilities, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing economic restrictions.
Tehran has accused Washington of failing to fulfill its commitments under the memorandum, including sanctions relief and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
Washington, for its part, has accused Tehran of failing to meet its obligations and has maintained economic pressure on Iran, arguing that sanctions are aimed at restricting revenue and financial networks that it says support Tehran’s military and regional activities.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones took Ryazan’s blending unit after knocking out two of its four crude units
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck the Ryazan oil refinery in Russia on the morning of 6 September and set one of its core units on fire, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported. The unit produces the high-octane component the Rosneft plant needs for its higher grades of gasoline. Russian regional authorities acknowledged a fire without naming the site. Ryazan is situated southeast of Moscow, about 470 km from Ukraine.
What burned at Ryazan
Drones hit the low-temperature isomerization unit for pentane-hexane fractions, designated Izomalk-2-LIN-800, according to Militarnyi's analysis. The unit sits on the refinery's grounds and is one of the critically important links in the plant's production cycle.
It converts low-octane straight-run oil fractions into a cleaner high-octane blending component. That component is what allows the refinery to produce gasolines of the higher environmental classes, Euro-5 among them, without adding harmful additives.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ published videos of the strike.
The same unit was hit in December
Drones already attacked this unit in December 2025 and damaged it. Earlier waves targeted the plant's ELOU-AVT-3, ELOU-AVT-6, and AVT-1 units.
By May 2026 the refinery had lost 90–100% of its refining capacity. Satellite imagery from 3 August 2026 showed Ukraine's Defense Forces had disabled two of the four crude distillation units on site.
Ukrainian drones struck the refinery in May, and FP-1 drones set it and a nearby warehouse burning in July.
Russian officials report a fire, not a target
Ryazan Oblast governor Pavel Malkov confirmed the region came under drone attack. Drone debris damaged residential buildings in Ryazan and Sapozhkovsky district, he stated, and a fire broke out at an enterprise he did not name. He said there were no casualties and that emergency services were working.
Russian news Telegram channel Astra said its analysis of photographs taken by residents established that the fire was on the grounds of the Ryazan refinery. Ukrainian channel Exilenova+, which tracks such attacks, also reported a hit on the plant.
Russia's fuel squeeze
Ukraine's General Staff said strikes on 26 August and 1 September fully stopped two large refining enterprises: Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez in Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, and the Novatek-Ust-Luga complex in Leningrad Oblast. Both supply the Russian army.
Short of gasoline, Russia has been buying more fuel abroad. Moscow discussed importing gasoline from Kazakhstan in June, and a Kazakh refinery deal would cover 0.3% of Russian demand. Belarus increased its gasoline supplies to Russia nearly 20-fold in the first half of the year.

articles.title: Far-right AfD wins key German state election but may fail to secure majority
articles.body:
The populist far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland has emerged as the winner in a crucial state election in Germany, exit polls have projected, but it remains unclear as to whether it will be able to form a government and become the first far-right party to gain power at regional or parliament level since the second world war.
Initial exit polls showed the party to have secured 44.5% of the vote, decisively ahead of the Christian Democrats of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in a contest that was being followed across the world.
The CDU was trailing massively on 18.5% and the far-left Die Linke was third with 9.5%, with the Social Democrats on 8% and the Greens on 9%. The smaller BSW reached the 5% hurdle needed to re-enter parliament, against expectations.
Participation was at a record high of 76.5%.
Votes are still being counted, but it appeared initially that the AfD might have failed to secure an absolute majority, the condition it has said is central to it taking power, as it refuses to govern with another party.
The CDU and all other mainstream parties have also refused to collude with the AfD in a government, in what is referred to as a Brandmauer, or firewall. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.
About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state of 2.1 million residents. Polling booths opened at 8am local time and closed at 6pm, when exit polls were released.
Final polls before the vote had shown the AfD to have around 40-41% of support. The party ended up doing even better than predicted but according to initial results appears to have fallen short of the goal of its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, to gain 45% or more.
Siegmund has consistently said he would refuse to take over as state premier unless his party gained an absolute majority, saying this was the only way it could effectively enact change in Germany.
The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed.
In a reflection of the significance of the vote for the entire German political landscape, the level of voter participation was considerably higher than at previous elections, hitting 54% by 2pm, compared with 27% at the same time for the equivalent vote five years ago, according to the state election commissioner.
The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties.
At a final rally on Saturday, he told supporters: “No matter the outcome of tomorrow’s election, we have already made history.”
The Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is unpopular, along with his government – a coalition with the SPD – having failed in his promises so far to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to the extent that it has appeased the average voter.
A win for the AfD puts huge pressure on Merz. In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has it eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033.
If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools, and halt the building of new windfarms.
He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools.
Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ostalgie” or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically.
Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”.
Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations planned. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”.
On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.”
The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said.
The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.
Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

articles.title: Ukraine, Europe and US to hold meeting in near future – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukraine, Europe and US to hold meeting in near future – Zelenskyy
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine, the US and Europe have agreed to hold another meeting involving their representatives.
Source: Zelenskyy after the conclusion of negotiations in Kyiv, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy noted that national security advisers to the leaders of France, the UK and Germany joined the Ukraine-US negotiations in Kyiv during the third round.
Quote: "We have agreed that Ukraine, Europe and America will meet in the near future.
I do not know where the meeting will be – in Europe, in the United States of America, or perhaps again – as I understood it, Steve liked our railways – so perhaps again in Ukraine. Well, we are open in any case".
Background:
- US presidential special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv by train on 6 September and met with the Ukrainian president at Sofiiska Square. After a tour inside St Sophia Cathedral, they proceeded to negotiations.
- Zelenskyy said that three rounds of negotiations took place on 6 September in total, and all of them were "very substantive" and discussions covered possible parameters for ending the war and short-term support for Ukraine.
- In remarks to the press after the first round of negotiations, Kushner stated that Trump is firmly determined to bring an end to the war.
- On 5 September, the special envoys held negotiations in Moscow. Yuri Ushakov, an aide to the Russian ruler, said Vladimir Putin told the US envoys during Saturday's talks that he is confident his war aims will be achieved. The White House described the talks as "substantive" and announced that the next steps will be unveiled in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Zelenskyy reveals details of talks with Trump envoys: winter package, territories, security guarantees
articles.body:
Zelenskyy reveals details of talks with Trump envoys: winter package, territories, security guarantees
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reported that, during talks in Kyiv with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and national security advisers from France, the UK and Germany, the discussions covered not only potential parameters for ending the war but also short-term support for Ukraine.
Source: Zelenskyy after the conclusion of negotiations, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy said that three rounds of negotiations took place on 6 September in total, and all of them were "very substantive".
The president joked that the presence of Witkoff and Kushner in Kyiv "worked better than Patriot systems" and said he hopes they will visit more often so that ordinary Ukrainians could have the chance to "live a little" without Russian attacks.
"One can sometimes joke about 'Patriot', but nonetheless, we understand that this is a very pressing issue, very important for us… If the war continues into winter – and for now it looks that way – we are very much counting on the 'winter package', which I discussed in detail today with Steve, Jared and our European partners," Zelenskyy said.
He noted that Kyiv is counting on air defence, energy support and the possibility of using American liquefied natural gas.
Quote: "The territorial question remains a pressing one… This does not mean we talked about it for a very long time, but we had the opportunity and we did discuss it. I will maintain my position that complex issues like this are resolved only at the level of leaders."
Details: Zelensky added that they also discussed security guarantees, economic guarantees, recovery and a "prosperity plan" for Ukraine.
"We understand what our armed forces must look like, they must be strong – and these are the main security guarantees for us. All of this requires resources. And you understand this perfectly well, we all understand this. Therefore, the guarantees must be strong and clear," the president said.
Background:
- The US presidential special envoys arrived in Kyiv by train on 6 September and met with the Ukrainian president at Sofiiska Square. After a tour inside St Sophia Cathedral, they proceeded to negotiations.
- In remarks to the press after the first round of negotiations, Kushner stated that Trump is firmly determined to bring an end to the war.
- Zelenskyy had previously announced that several negotiating sessions would take place in Kyiv: first with the US presidential envoys, then with the participation of negotiators from France, the UK and Germany.
